title: Projects
text:
Culture is present not just in humans but in a wide range of other species. My current work centers around building the Animal Culture Database (ACDB), which aims to document cultural behaviors such as song dialects, foraging traditions, and migratory knowledge in wild animal populations worldwide and evidence for human impacts on these behaviors. The first version of the database was introduced in a 2025 paper. You can find the GitHub repository here and the web app to browse the database here. It’s currently in its initial stages and very incomplete, but I plan to expand it to cover the entirety of the literature on culture across animal species with a contributions pipeline for new data.



I’ve recently begun collaborating with Dr. Mason Youngblood on an updated bibliometric analysis of his 2018 paper. For future work, I also plan to research historical and ideological factors influencing the reception of cultural evolutionary theory and methods in other academic fields.



I’m interested in applying text analytic and other quantitative methods to historical, archaeological, and ethnographic data to measure how what we now diagnose as discrete mental disorders have varied across times and cultures. Please get in touch if this is something you’d be interested in collaborating on!

title: Projects
text:
Historical wartime violence
My doctoral research was on how forms of wartime violence, including indiscriminate killing of enemies, trophy-taking practices, and self-sacrificial behavior, varied cross-culturally among historical societies.

title: Projects
text:
Evolution of cephalopod intelligence
Cephalopods (squids, octopuses, and cuttlefish) are primarily asocial invertebrates very distantly related to humans. They are fascinating in their own right, and, because of their evolutionary distance from social vertebrates such as birds and mammals, are a phylogenetically interesting group with which to examine the evolution of cognition. I was fortunate to be involved with a Diverse Intelligences project examining the drivers of brain evolution across cephalopods. Paper: Ecological not social factors explain brain size in cephalopods

title: Projects
text:
Phylogeny of Islamic traditions
My MSc research applied phylogenetic methods to model the cultural transmission of afterlife beliefs among historical Islamic sects. Paper: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-020-01013-4
Cultural phylogenetics of afterlife beliefs

title: Kiran Basava
text: My research uses comparative methods to explore macroevolutionary patterns of behavior and cognition in humans and other animals. Broadly, I am interested in how people (including animals) conceptualize ourselves and others in our social world, and how these cognitive capacities and the behaviors they give rise to have biologically and culturally evolved. I am currently a postdoctoral researcher with the Data Diversity Lab at the University of Arizona, where I am building the Animal Culture Database (ACDB), a global database of nonhuman animal cultures. Please visit my Google Scholar page to view my publications and Projects to learn more about my work.
